query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that integrates configurational entropy measures and atomic mass/fluctuation descriptors will more accurately identify high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity by capturing how severe chemical disorder and lattice distortion enhance phonon scattering.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-principal element (high-entropy) alloys with disordered crystalline structures featuring significant atomic mass contrast and lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Apply the predictive method—which uses enhanced descriptors (e.g., configurational entropy, mass contrast, and indicators from simulated phonon density-of-states) to screen candidate HEAs—to select and design compositions with maximized disorder-induced phonon scattering.
generation.conditions: Measurements are to be performed near operating temperatures relevant for thermal insulation, under quiescent conditions (i.e., without external mechanical loading) to isolate phonon transport phenomena.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced configurational entropy coupled with marked differences in atomic mass and force constants produces severe lattice distortions, leading to increased phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: The approach works because the detailed descriptors capture the disorder-induced lattice perturbations that scatter phonons more effectively, thereby reducing the phonon mean free path and lowering thermal conductivity beyond what traditional averaged-property models can predict.
generation.predicted_outcome: The predictive model is expected to outperform traditional heuristic predictions by more reliably identifying HEAs with a reduction in phonon thermal conductivity on the order of 20–30% relative to materials selected by conventional methods.
generation.baseline: Current prediction models rely mainly on heuristic phase diagrams and averaged thermophysical properties that do not fully account for the specific effects of chemical disorder and mass fluctuations in HEAs.
generation.boundary: The approach is likely to be most effective for multi-component systems with significant atomic mass differences and high configurational entropy; it may be less applicable to alloys with nearly identical constituent masses or low configurational disorder.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in prediction accuracy and the precise magnitude of thermal conductivity reduction remain uncertain, as they depend on the accuracy of the chosen descriptors and the model's ability to generalize across diverse HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of HEA samples selected by the new predictive approach and a comparable set chosen by conventional methods. Measure their phonon thermal conductivity using techniques such as inelastic neutron scattering or time-domain thermoreflectance under controlled temperature conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEAs identified by the predictive approach do not consistently demonstrate at least a 20% lower phonon thermal conductivity than those selected by traditional methods, or if the correlation between the predicted disorder metrics and reduced conductivity is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Exploring thermophysical properties of CoCrFeNiCu high entropy alloy via molecular dynamics simulations

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys composed of five or more primary elements in equal or nearly equal proportions of atoms. In the present study, the thermophysical properties of the CoCrFeNiCu high entropy alloy (HEA) were investigated by a molecular dynamics (MD) method at nanoscale. The effects of the content of individual elements on lattice thermal conductivity kp were revealed, and the results suggested that adjusting the atomic content can be a way to control the lattice thermal conductivity of HEAs. The effects of temperature on kp were investigated quantitively, and a power-law relationship of kp with T−0.419 was suggested, which agrees with previous findings. The effects of temperature and the content of individual elements on volumetric specific heat capacity Cv were also studied: as the temperature increases, the Cv of all HEAs slightly decreases and then increases. Phonon behavior in a random solid solution: a lattice dynamics study on the high-entropy alloy FeCoCrMnNi

Abstract: AbstractHigh-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) are a new family of crystalline random alloys with four or more elements in a simple unit cell, at the forefront of materials research for their exceptional mechanical properties. Their strong chemical disorder leads to mass and force-constant fluctuations which are expected to strongly reduce phonon lifetime, responsible for thermal transport, similarly to glasses. Still, the long range order would associate HEAs to crystals with a complex disordered unit cell. These two families of materials, however, exhibit very different phonon dynamics, still leading to similar thermal properties. The question arises on the positioning of HEAs in this context. Here we present an exhaustive experimental investigation of the lattice dynamics in a HEA, Fe20Co20Cr20Mn20Ni20, using inelastic neutron and X-ray scattering. We demonstrate that HEAs present unique phonon dynamics at the frontier between fully disordered and ordered materials, characterized by long-propagating acoustic phonons in the whole Brillouin zone.Subject terms: Electronic proper
